land.text: Nicaragua, which left the Federal Republic of Central America on 30 April 1838 ('Nicaragua definitively became an independent republic in 1838')

predecessors.note: The Mosquito Coast strip was a British-protected kingdom throughout and joined Nicaragua only as an autonomous reserve in 1860.

capitals.name: Managua
capitals.note: Managua 'rose to undisputed preeminence as the nation's capital in 1852' to end the rivalry between León and Granada.

correction.text: Nicaragua without the Mosquito Coast strip: Cliopatria's 1846 shape (111,716 km2), the land outside the British-protected Mosquito Kingdom

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria begins in 1840; the infobox dates Nicaragua's exit from the federation to 30 April 1838. The strip east of about 83.6 W is left out because the Mosquito Coast page has the kingdom under a British protectorate ('Treaty of Friendship and Alliance in 1740') until the Treaty of Managua of 28 January 1860.

correction.text: Nicaragua without the Mosquito Coast strip: Cliopatria's 1846 shape (111,716 km2), the land outside the British-protected Mosquito Kingdom

keyframe_review.note: The 132,580 km2 shape holds the Mosquito Coast (17,450 km2 more than the 1846 shape on the cell grid) as Nicaraguan, but the Mosquito Coast page has it a British-protected kingdom until the 28 January 1860 treaty transferred suzerainty, not full sovereignty, to Nicaragua; the dossier uses the 1846 shape for 1840-1845. Infobox area 130,375 km2 is for the modern country, so the full shape is not wrong for it (ratio 1.02) but is wrong for these years. The page gives no event for Cliopatria's 1846 step.

correction.text: Nicaragua without the Mosquito Coast strip: Cliopatria's 1846 shape (111,716 km2), the land outside the British-protected Mosquito Kingdom

keyframe_review.note: Same outline as 1840-1841 (132,580 km2 including the Mosquito Coast); the page dates the Miskito king's claim to San Juan del Norte to August 1841, with 'all Nicaraguan forces' still there until 1 January 1848. The 1846 shape is used for 1842-1845.

111,716 km2 without the Mosquito strip (ratio 0.86 to the infobox's 130,375 km2; the strip is about 17,950 km2). The kingdom is the page's British-protected Mosquito Kingdom; the 7 March 1848 cession of San Juan del Norte is below the grid (the 1846 and 1853 shapes are identical on the H3 grid), so the ledger carries it. The Mosquito Coast page dates the step that Cliopatria draws in 1846: 'In 1844, the British government declared a new protectorate over the Mosquito Kingdom' (reviewer am-08-f).

111,425 km2, 291 km2 less than 1846 and identical to it on the cell grid; the pages opened give no 1853 event (the Mosquito Kingdom row begins in 1853; the page's only 1850s items are the Clayton-Bulwer Treaty of 18 April 1850 and the bombardment of Greytown in 1854).

correction.text: the 1857 shape (111,425 km2) held through 1856: Nicaragua under William Walker, who declared himself president after a sham election in 1856 and was inaugurated on 12 July 1856

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria has no Nicaragua shape for 1856. Its 'Republic of Baja California' row has a 1856 shape (111,425 km2, bbox -87.66..-83.57, 10.70..14.81) that is cell for cell Nicaragua's, so Cliopatria draws Walker's Nicaragua under that Name; the Baja California dossier should drop its 1856 shape.
111,425 km2, the 1853 outline; Walker surrendered on 1 May 1857 and the Legitimist government returned. The Mosquito strip is still outside (until 1860).

correction.text: the 1861 shape (111,452 km2) for 1860: Nicaragua gained only suzerainty, not full sovereignty, over the Mosquito coast under the Treaty of Managua of 28 January 1860, which became an autonomous reserve; the strip is drawn as a vassal tint by the ledger's vassal events, not as direct land

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria's 1860 shape (132,580 km2) is the whole modern country, but the page keeps the Reserve autonomous until 20 November 1894 and the 1861-1894 shape leaves it out; the 1860 shape is cut to the same outline so the vassal tint carries the Reserve for 1860-1894.

111,452 km2 without the Mosquito Reserve (about 17,950 km2 on the cell grid; 111,452 + 17,950 = 129,400 km2 against the infobox's 130,375 km2, ratio 0.99). Drawn as direct Nicaraguan land only; the Reserve is a vassal from 28 January 1860 to 20 November 1894 in the ledger.

132,555 km2: the Reserve is inside after 'formally became incorporated into that of the republic of Nicaragua' on 20 November 1894 under Zelaya (renamed the Zelaya Department). Cliopatria's outline has 49 vertices against 44 for the 1898 shape; they are identical on the grid.

132,580 km2 against the infobox's 130,375 km2 (ratio 1.02); the Honduran frontier along the Coco (granted to Honduras by the ICJ in 1960, Mosquito Coast page) and the Costa Rican frontier on the San Juan River are not distinguishable from the constant outline, so the shape stands for 1898-2023.
Same outline as 1898-2023; infobox area 130,375 km2.

region.text: Nicaragua without the Mosquito Coast strip: Cliopatria's 1846 shape (111,716 km2), the land outside the British-protected Mosquito Kingdom

ledger.note: 1838: Nicaragua leaves the Federal Republic of Central America. Infobox 'From the Federal Republic of Central America: 30 April 1838'; 'Nicaragua definitively became an independent republic in 1838'. The page names the country, not the Mosquito strip; the strip is left out on the Mosquito Coast page's evidence.

region.text: San Juan del Norte (Greytown) at the mouth of the San Juan River

ledger.note: 1848: Miskito and British forces seize San Juan del Norte. The Miskito king's ultimatum demanded that 'all Nicaraguan forces' leave 'before 1 January 1848'; after it expired Miskito-British forces seized the port (no day given). The king had claimed the town from a British ship in August 1841.

region.text: San Juan del Norte (Greytown) at the mouth of the San Juan River

ledger.note: 1848: Nicaragua cedes San Juan del Norte. On 7 March 1848 Nicaragua signed a peace treaty ceding San Juan del Norte to the Mosquito Kingdom, which renamed it Greytown.

region.text: San Juan del Norte (Greytown) at the mouth of the San Juan River

ledger.note: 1848: the dispute over San Juan del Norte ends with the peace treaty of 7 March 1848.
1852: Managua becomes the capital. It 'rose to undisputed preeminence as the nation's capital in 1852' to end the rivalry between León and Granada.

1855: Walker and the Democrats take Granada and the government. on 13 October 1855 Walker and the Democrats captured Granada; on 23 October Corral signs a peace treaty, Patricio Rivas became president with Walker as commander-in-chief, though Walker holds the real power. The state and its colour continue; no land changes hands.

region.text: Virgin Bay and the Transit Route country on the western shore of Lake Nicaragua, taken by Costa Rican forces on 7 April 1856

ledger.note: 1856: Costa Rican forces enter Nicaragua. Costa Rica declared war on Walker's government on 27 February 1856, won at Santa Rosa on 20 March and took Virgin Bay on 7 April 1856. The page does not say how long they stayed, so the Rivas department is the researcher's reading of the zone (Costa Rica's dossier carries the same pair).

1856: William Walker takes the presidency of Nicaragua. On 12 July 1856 Walker was inaugurated as president; he declared himself president after a sham election in 1856 (Nicaragua page). Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras had formed the Allied Central American Army with the Legitimists. The state and its colour continue; Cliopatria draws this year under the Name 'Republic of Baja California'.
1857: Walker surrenders and the Legitimist government returns. on 1 May 1857 Walker surrendered to US Navy commander Charles Henry Davis, who offered safe passage out of the country.

region.text: Virgin Bay and the Transit Route country on the western shore of Lake Nicaragua, taken by Costa Rican forces on 7 April 1856

ledger.note: 1857: Walker surrenders on 1 May 1857 and the war ends; Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras had fought beside the Nicaraguan Legitimists.

region.text: the coast between Cabo Gracias a Dios and Greytown (the Mosquito Coast strip of about 17,950 km2 that Cliopatria draws outside Nicaragua in 1846-1859 and 1861-1894)

ledger.note: 1860: Britain hands the Mosquito coast to Nicaraguan suzerainty. Britain and Nicaragua 'signed the Treaty of Managua on 28 January 1860', transferring suzerainty, not full sovereignty, over the coast between Cabo Gracias a Dios and Greytown; the Mosquito Kingdom, 'now reduced to the territory around Bluefields', became an autonomous reserve. The page also has Britain cede the northern coast to Honduras in 1859. The strip is Cliopatria's, a reading of the page's 'coast'.

region.text: the northern bank of the Coco (Wanks) River, the 21 cells of Honduras's Gracias a Dios department that Cliopatria draws in the Mosquito Kingdom, around Cape Gracias a Dios (the Honduras dossier's zone)

ledger.note: 1869: the northern boundary of the Mosquito coast along the Coco (Wanks) River becomes disputed. 'The northern boundary along the Coco (Wanks) River was disputed from 1869 onward' (the page: the dispute began 'ninety-one years' before 1960). A boundary dispute, not a campaign; the zone is the Honduran dossier's.

region.text: the coast between Cabo Gracias a Dios and Greytown (the Mosquito Coast strip of about 17,950 km2 that Cliopatria draws outside Nicaragua in 1846-1859 and 1861-1894)

ledger.note: 1894: the Mosquito Reserve ends. On 20 November 1894 the territory 'formally became incorporated into that of the republic of Nicaragua' under José Santos Zelaya; the United States had occupied Bluefields from 6 July to 7 August 1894.

region.text: the coast between Cabo Gracias a Dios and Greytown (the Mosquito Coast strip of about 17,950 km2 that Cliopatria draws outside Nicaragua in 1846-1859 and 1861-1894)

ledger.note: 1894: Zelaya incorporates the Mosquito Reserve. Nicaragua page: Mosquitia stayed semi-independent until José Santos Zelaya's government occupied it 'militarily' in the Nicaragua Crisis of 1894-1895, and Zelaya then renamed it the Zelaya Department.

1912: United States Marines occupy Nicaragua. The occupation lasted until 1933 'with one break of about nine months starting in 1925'; the page gives no month for either end. Nicaragua stayed formally sovereign; the Bryan-Chamorro Treaty of 1914 gave the US canal rights.
1933: the US Marines leave Nicaragua after the occupation of 1912-1933 (a nine-month break began in 1925).

region.text: the northern bank of the Coco (Wanks) River, the 21 cells of Honduras's Gracias a Dios department that Cliopatria draws in the Mosquito Kingdom, around Cape Gracias a Dios (the Honduras dossier's zone)

ledger.note: 1960: the International Court of Justice settles the northern bank. 'In 1960 the northern part was granted to Honduras by the International Court of Justice.'

region.text: the northern bank of the Coco (Wanks) River, the 21 cells of Honduras's Gracias a Dios department that Cliopatria draws in the Mosquito Kingdom, around Cape Gracias a Dios (the Honduras dossier's zone)

ledger.note: 1960: the northern part of the Mosquito Coast goes to Honduras. The page names no cells; Cliopatria's Nicaragua outline never held this land (it is drawn in the Mosquito Kingdom 1846-1859 and in Honduras), so the event moves no cell of Nicaragua's shape and is recorded for the counterpart in the Honduras dossier (gain from republic-of-nicaragua, 1960).

wars.name: Filibuster War
wars.outcome: Walker, commissioned colonel in June 1855, took Granada on 13 October 1855, was inaugurated president on 12 July 1856 and surrendered on 1 May 1857 to the Allied Central American Army and the Legitimists; he was executed at Trujillo on 12 September 1860.
wars.note: No border moved; Costa Rica's dossier carries the contested Rivas/Virgin Bay zone. Legitimists captured Granada on 12 October 1856 while Walker was at Masaya.

wars.name: San Juan del Norte dispute with the Mosquito Kingdom and Britain

zones.text: San Juan del Norte (Greytown) at the mouth of the San Juan River

wars.outcome: The Miskito king's claim of August 1841 and ultimatum of 1 January 1848 ended with Nicaragua ceding San Juan del Norte on 7 March 1848.
wars.note: The Clayton-Bulwer Treaty of 18 April 1850 and the bombardment of Greytown by USS Cyane in 1854 follow.

wars.name: Honduras-Nicaragua border dispute

zones.text: the northern bank of the Coco (Wanks) River, the 21 cells of Honduras's Gracias a Dios department that Cliopatria draws in the Mosquito Kingdom, around Cape Gracias a Dios (the Honduras dossier's zone)

wars.outcome: Disputed from 1869; King Alfonso XIII of Spain awarded the disputed area to Honduras in 1906 (Honduras's view); 'In 1960 the northern part was granted to Honduras by the International Court of Justice'.
wars.note: The 1906 award is from the Honduras-Nicaragua border page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honduras–Nicaragua_border), which gives the year only. The ledger carries the contest (1869-1960) and the 1960 loss to match the Honduras dossier.

wars.name: Costa Rica-Nicaragua border settlement (Cañas-Jerez Treaty)

zones.text: the San Juan River frontier: the treaty 'puts the border on the right bank of the river, giving the river to Nicaragua'

wars.outcome: The treaty enacted on 15 April 1858 fixed the frontier from the south of Lake Nicaragua east along the San Juan River; President Cleveland recognised it on 22 March 1888.
wars.note: No land changed hands on the page; the Mosquito Coast, Honduras and Costa Rica frontiers are the dossier's only treaty lines before 1960.

wars.name: US occupation of Nicaragua
wars.outcome: US Marines occupied Nicaragua from 1912 to 1933 with a nine-month break starting in 1925; the 1914 Bryan-Chamorro Treaty gave the US canal rights; no cession.

wars.name: Nicaraguan Revolution and Contra war
wars.outcome: 'The Sandinistas forcefully took power in July 1979, ousting Somoza'; the Contras operated in the 1980s from camps in Honduras and Costa Rica. No border moved.
wars.note: The page dates the Contra war only as 'the 1980s'.

certainty.note: The Mosquito coast was a protectorate or reserve (1838-1894), the Honduran boundary on the Coco was disputed from 1869 to 1960, and the Costa Rican frontier is the exception: sharp from the 1858 Cañas-Jerez Treaty and the 1888 Cleveland Award.

'In 1960 the northern part was granted to Honduras by the International Court of Justice'; the mouth of the San Juan River (Costa Rica) and the Colombian archipelago claims stay disputed (Nicaragua page).

notes: Pages: five (budget). Judgment calls: (1) the Mosquito strip (Cliopatria's 1840-1845 shapes include it, 1846+ do not) is left out for 1838-1859 on the evidence of the Mosquito Coast page (British-protected kingdom until the Treaty of Managua), and drawn as a vassal tint 28 January 1860 - 20 November 1894 (Cliopatria's 1860 shape gives it as direct land). The page gives no event for Cliopatria's 1846 step. (2) Walker's regime is a 'rename' (same state, new regime) at 1855/10, 1856/7 and 1857/5, not a rebel state; Cliopatria's 1856 shape sits in its 'Republic of Baja California' row (a Nicaragua shape in everything but the Name) and the Baja California dossier should not also draw it. (3) The mosquito-kingdom dossier (another part) should run its vassal life to 1894, not end in 1859 as Cliopatria's row does; the seed lists british-colonial-empire as Nicaragua's neighbour in 1846-1852, which is probably Cliopatria's drawing of the British protectorate. (4) The 1869-1960 Coco River dispute and the 1960 transfer to Honduras are ledger events to match the Honduras dossier, but Cliopatria's Nicaragua outline never held that land (21 cells, drawn in the Mosquito Kingdom and Honduras), so they move no cell; the 1906 award is on the border page by year only. (5) Capital 1838-1851 is not given by the page (León and Granada rivalry); no capital entry for those years. (6) The Legitimist-Democrat fighting before Walker's arrival and the Corn Islands, San Andrés and Providencia questions are not dated or described by the pages opened. Gazetteer: San Juan del Norte resolves through the alias of San Juan de Nicaragua; no new names.
